title: How Roche's Founder Shared His Firm to Save It in 1919
dek: After war and revolution took Roche's biggest market, Fritz Hoffmann turned his family firm into a limited company with outside money, and died a year later.

story.event: Rescuing the company as a limited company after losing the Russian market
story.summary: After the First World War cut Roche off from its German factory and the Russian Revolution of 1917 took away what the company calls its biggest market, F. Hoffmann-La Roche & Co. was near bankruptcy by 1919. With support from the Basler Handelsbank, headed by Fritz Hoffmann's brother-in-law, the firm was converted into a limited company in 1919. Hoffmann, whose health had worsened from 1918, died on 18 April 1920; his successor Emil Barell cut half the workforce, and the capital was doubled in 1920.
paragraphs: In 1910 Roche opened a branch in St Petersburg. Fritz Hoffmann, from a Basel merchant family, had founded the drug company in 1896 and travelled to Russia himself to build trade there, and by the company's own account Russia became Roche's biggest market. By 1912 Roche had branches in nine countries on three continents, selling medicines such as the heart drug Digalen and the painkiller Pantopon with advertising on a scale new for its day.

The First World War broke that network apart. The Basel works were cut off from the larger factory across the German border at Grenzach. Germans called the firm French-leaning because of its Paris branch, the French called it German because of Grenzach, and it was blacklisted in both countries. Then the Russian Revolution of 1917 took away the Russian market, which Roche's history calls a far heavier blow. After the war, its funds in Germany were blocked and German inflation was beginning. By 1919, the company says, Roche was near bankruptcy and needed capital at once.

Hoffmann's answer was to stop being the firm's sole master. In 1919, with the support of the Basler Handelsbank, whose president was his brother-in-law Albert Koechlin, the family business became a limited company, F. Hoffmann-La Roche & Co. Ltd. Hoffmann kept the management as vice-chairman and delegate of the board, and set about reopening the foreign connections the war had cut. The strain showed. By Roche's account his health had worsened sharply from 1918, and in 1919 he and his wife Adèle ended their marriage.

He did not see the recovery. Fritz Hoffmann died in Basel on 18 April 1920, aged 52. Emil Barell, a chemist who had joined in 1896, took over and, according to the company, had to dismiss half the workforce. In 1920 shareholders were asked to double the capital. The Hoffmann family could not find enough money, the Swiss broadcaster SRF reported in 2021, and the Basler Handelsbank became the largest shareholder; the heirs won back a majority only at the end of the 1930s. The company that nearly failed in 1919 became one of the world's largest makers of medicines and diagnostic tests.

quote.text: We should therefore praise, and number in the company of the blest, that man who has invested well the portion of time, however little, that has been allotted to him; for such a one has seen the true light.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.locator: Letter XCIII, "On the Quality, as Contrasted with the Length, of Life", section 5
quote.source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 93, tr. Richard M. Gummere (Wikisource)
quote.connection: Hoffmann died at 52, a year after the rescue and before anyone knew whether it would hold. Seneca, writing to a friend who mourned an early death, argues that a life is measured by what was done with its time, not by how long it lasted.

reflection: The record does not say what it cost Hoffmann to turn the company that bore his name into one he no longer owned alone. It does show the order in which things went: first a market, then the money, then his health and his marriage. He took help from his brother-in-law's bank before the firm failed, not after.

Seneca would not measure his life by its fifty-two years. There is something plainer in it for you as well. When pressure comes from several sides at once, sharing the load early is a decision, not a defeat, and the tiredness you carry belongs in the reckoning with everything else.
invitation: Name one thing you are carrying alone that someone you trust could share, and ask them about it this week, before it has to become an emergency.

sources.title: Our history

Barell; later world leadership in in-vitro diagnostics after 1997

cross_checks.claim: Loss of the Russian market after the 1917 revolution pushed Roche into a deep financial crisis
In 1919 the firm was converted into a limited (joint-stock) company to survive
The Basler Handelsbank, headed by Hoffmann's brother-in-law Albert Koechlin, supported the rescue
During the war Roche was boycotted or blacklisted in both France and Germany
Fritz Hoffmann died in Basel on 18 April 1920 and Emil Barell succeeded him
In 1920 the share capital had to be doubled

research_notes: Ownership after 1919 is where the sources disagree. Roche's own history (2016) says the founder retained only a minority interest in the new limited company. The International Directory of Company Histories (via Encyclopedia.com) says Hoffmann himself supplied 3 million of the 4 million francs of paid-in capital, with the rest from his brother-in-law, two associates and Barell, which would imply a majority. SRF (2021) places the family's loss of the majority after his death, when the capital was doubled and the Basler Handelsbank became the largest shareholder. Because these cannot be reconciled from the sources, the story does not state Hoffmann's stake in 1919, says only that he stopped being the firm's sole master, and gives SRF's account of the 1920s shareholding with attribution. The Directory also gives a loss of 'more than 1 million francs' in uncollected Russian receivables; no other source gives a figure, so the story uses none. Size of the Russian market: Roche's history says Russia had become Roche's biggest market; the Riga Stradins University paper abstract calls it the second-largest. The story attributes 'biggest' to the company. The bank's head is named Rudolf Albert Koechlin-Hoffmann by Roche and Albert Koechlin (1859-1927), president of Basler Handelsbank and husband of Hoffmann's sister Elisabeth, by the NDB; the story uses 'Albert Koechlin'. The halving of the workforce under Barell rests on Roche's own history and is attributed to the company; it is dated only as 'at first' after Barell took over, so the story places it after Hoffmann's death without giving a year. Pharmaphorum's history was read but not cited because it misdates the start of the First World War to 1915. The Directory's account also contains errors elsewhere (it credits Barell with developing Thiocol, which the NDB attributes to the chemist Carl Schaerges in 1897), so it is used only for points matched by another source. No first-hand statement by Hoffmann about the decision was found; the story describes only what he did. The Seneca letter consoles Lucilius over the death of the philosopher Metronax and is applied here by analogy.
